newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE-Singapore could gain from HK handover.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Singapore could gain from HK handover.

text.p: Singapore's efforts to position itself as a regional financial and business powerhouse could receive a lift from the return of Hong Kong to China, but the gains are likely to be slow and hard-won, analysts say.
The similarities between the two bustling free-market economies have long drawn comparison, particularly in areas like port services, tourism, banking and finance, where they compete head on.

While Singapore officials turn coy at any mention of rivalry, quickly citing each territory's strengths, efforts to market Singapore to Hong Kong residents began much before the British colony's scheduled July 1, 1997 handover to China.

Under a special scheme Singapore launched soon after China's brutal crackdown on student-led democracy movements in Beijing in June 1989, Hong Kong Chinese given approval-in-principle can immigrate to Singapore within five years. The status is renewable and no investment is needed.
Unofficial estimates place the number of Hong Kong families in Singapore at over 7,000.
Last July, Singapore organised an unprecedented three-day exhibition in Hong Kong, seeking to promote Singapore's lifestyle, government-sponsored housing and business opportunities.
TWO CITIES AS TWIN HUBS
How Peck Huat, director of East Asia at the Singapore Economic Development Board office in Hong Kong, said the two cities are distinct hubs which complement each other.

"Companies have positioned themselves to have twin regional headquarters, one in Hong Kong to handle East Asia and another in Singapore to handle Southeast Asia. So it's not a question of taking from one and giving to the other," How said.
"Occasionally if a company only needs one headquarters, it has to decide whether Hong Kong or Singapore is a better bet to cover Asia. Then of course we hope it would be Singapore," How added.
His view appeared to be borne out by Gary Coull, chairman of Credit Lyonnais Securities Asia in Hong Kong.

"We have a big operation in Singapore...We're very happy to expand our Southeast Asian business from there. We find it more convenient to have our North Asian business based in Hong Kong," Coull said.
He said Singapore's strengths included its education system, a high standard of English and long-term plans to develop as a high technology and services centre.

But Hong Kong's future was assured simply by its proximity to the Chinese economy, which would explode over the next couple of decades, and there was little Singapore could do to compete against this, he added.
SINGAPORE'S GROWING PULL

"There's growing evidence that while the bulk of fund management and banking in Asia, excluding Japan is still concentrated in Hong Kong, the number of companies opening up in Singapore has been on the increase," said a senior economist with a large European bank in Singapore.
He said Singapore had been very successful in establishing itself as a regional foreign exchange and fixed income centre, despite tight restrictions on trading of its own currency.

Of Singapore's average daily foreign exchange turnover of US$130 billion last year, only about six percent involved trading in the Singapore dollar, Finance Minister Richard Hu said in a speech last month.

He said there were nearly 700 banks and financial institutions in Singapore and 34 multinational companies had set up regional finance and treasury centres here. Companies with Singapore-based regional treasury operations are entitled to a concessionary tax rate of 10 percent.

"Singapore's attractiveness is more for foreign direct investors. For companies with manufacturing plants in Vietnam, China or India, Singapore offers fantastic infrastructure to set up their headquarters," said Dilip Ratha, senior economist at W.I. Carr in Singapore.
He said Singapore was likely to benefit from Hong Kong's handover further down the road, particularly if there was any sense of China tightening its grip over the territory.
"People are still holding on in Hong Kong; they are waiting to see how things will evolve. My guess is the real wave of migration may happen around July 1998," Ratha said.

"Slowly we'll see China taking over and that's not neccesarily inconsistent wih prosperity or continuity in Hong Kong, but there are concerns about the situation after a year or two of China's rule in Hong Kong," he said.

Singapore statesman Lee Kuan Yew, a frequent commentator on China, said recently Hong Kong's people would not agitate for more democracy after the territory's handover as China was too powerful to be swayed by such appeals.
"If you don't believe that the Hong Kong people understand that, then you don't understand Hong Kong," Lee was quoted as saying by the daily Straits Times newspaper last week.
Lee led Singapore to independence from the British in the early 1960s and was Singapore's prime minister until 1990. He remains in the government as senior minister.
